q: After a power-failure event, the department adds a battery-charge check to the daily machine checklist. Which risk management step is this?
c: Estimating likelihood
Defining potential problems
Monitoring
Applying solutions
exp: Risk management steps: define potential problems, estimate likelihood, weigh the benefits of expending resources, apply solutions, and monitor. Adding the battery check is the solution; tracking whether it prevents future problems would be monitoring.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 16, 25 (PDF p. 8, 13)

q: The ETT has been pulled and gases stopped during an airway fire. Which sequence of the NEXT steps matches the lecture?
c: Mask ventilate first, then remove burning material, then saline
Saline into the airway, remove burning material, mask ventilate, then assess
Bronchoscopy first, then pour saline, then mask ventilate
Reintubate right away, then pour saline, then mask ventilate
exp: After simultaneously removing the tube and stopping gases: pour saline into the airway, remove burning material, mask ventilate, assess for injury, consider bronchoscopy, and reintubate.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 36 (PDF p. 18)

q: Which are reported causes of total breathing-circuit OCCLUSION (as opposed to leaks)? Select 3.
c: A disposable swivel connector crack
A vaporizer filler cap left loose
Plastic wrapping left on a component
A freestanding PEEP valve in the inspiratory limb
An incorrectly connected humidifier
A loose ETT connection under the drapes
exp: Reported occlusion causes: filters in the circuit, incorrectly connected humidifiers, manufacturing defects, failure to remove plastic wrapping, and a freestanding PEEP valve placed in the inspiratory limb. Loose connections, cracked connectors, and loose filler caps cause leaks, not occlusion.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 22 (PDF p. 11)

q: In an OR with ungrounded (isolated) power, a staff member touches one energized conductor while standing on the floor. Why is macroshock less likely than it would be at home?
c: Isolated power converts the AC supply into safer DC
The ungrounded supply runs at a much lower voltage
The equipment's ground wire blocks the current path
No path to ground exists, so no current flows through them
exp: In the OR's ungrounded system, current is isolated from ground potential. Touching a single conductor doesn't complete a circuit through the body to ground, which is the added macroshock protection the lecture describes. At home, power is grounded, so the same contact can complete a circuit.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 29, 30 (PDF p. 15)

q: On a machine whose proportioning system links only O2 and N2O, flows are O2 1 L/min, N2O 3 L/min, and pure helium 2 L/min. What is the delivered FiO2?
c: About 17%
About 21%
About 25%
About 33%
exp: The proportioner is satisfied (O2 is 25% of O2 + N2O), but helium adds volume without O2: 1 L O2 in 6 L total is about 17%. This is the lecture's warning that helium with O2 plus added N2O can deliver less than 21%.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 14 (PDF p. 7)

q: For right shoulder surgery, the ESU return pad has been placed on the left calf and ECG pads on the right chest. What is the problem?
c: Nothing; the pad should always be as far from the site as possible
The ECG pads must be placed on the return pad
The pad on the left side will prevent the ESU from working
The current path is long and runs near the ECG; pad should be close to the site, ECG far
exp: Place the return plate as close as possible to the operative site and ECG pads as far away as feasible. A left calf pad for right shoulder surgery sends current across the body, and ECG pads near the site pick up interference.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 31 (PDF p. 16)

q: During MAC for a facial procedure, why does the lecture say to configure the drapes carefully?
c: To keep O2 from pooling under drapes near the ignition source
To keep ECG leads from dislodging under the drapes
To keep the patient warmer during the procedure
To let the ESU return pad sit close to the face
exp: Configure surgical drapes to minimize the buildup of oxidizer, and take extra care with open O2 delivery near the airway. O2 trapped under drapes creates an oxidizer-rich pocket right where cautery is used.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 35 (PDF p. 18)

q: Which hypoxemia hazards on slide 19 are NOT highlighted as usually caught on the machine check? Select 3.
c: Cylinder filled with hypoxic gas
Disconnected O2 hose at the wall
Crossed hospital pipelines
Liquid O2 reservoir filled with nitrogen
Breathing circuit leak at a connection
Empty O2 cylinder on the machine yoke
exp: Upstream supply problems and hypoxic gas inside a cylinder aren't highlighted; a machine check can't easily detect that a gas is the wrong gas. Empty cylinders, circuit leaks, and disconnected hoses are highlighted as usually caught on the check. That's why the O2 analyzer matters even after a clean check.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 19 (PDF p. 10)

q: The inspiratory unidirectional valve sticks open. What happens during exhalation?
c: Exhaled gas bypasses the absorber into the scavenger
The reservoir bag collapses completely
Exhaled gas flows back into the inspiratory limb and is rebreathed
Fresh gas is vented through the APL before reaching the patient
exp: Unidirectional valves keep gas moving one way around the circle. With the inspiratory valve incompetent, exhaled CO2-rich gas can move backward into the inspiratory limb and be inhaled with the next breath, a hypercarbia hazard listed on slide 20.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 20 (PDF p. 10)

q: Whenever cautery is used, SpO2 drops briefly and the ECG shows a chaotic rhythm, both normalizing when cautery stops. Which statements are correct? Select 2.
c: The patient is having intermittent V-fib from ESU current
The patient is desaturating from ESU-induced shunting
ESU energy is interfering with the pulse oximeter
The return pad needs to move closer to the ECG pads
ESU energy is interfering with the ECG
The pulse oximeter probe should be placed on the return pad
exp: The Bovie's high-frequency energy interferes with the ECG, pulse oximeters, cardiac output computers, and pacemakers. Changes that appear only with cautery and resolve when it stops are interference. ESU frequencies don't cause V-fib, and the ECG belongs far from the pad.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 31 (PDF p. 16)

q: Two O2 cylinders on a double yoke are both left open, one at 2000 psig and one at 500 psig. Which statements are correct? Select 2.
c: The shared gauge can't show the two cylinder pressures separately
Transfilling only occurs with N2O cylinders
Gas can transfill from the higher- to the lower-pressure cylinder
The shared gauge shows the average of the two cylinders
The first-stage regulator stops transfilling
The yoke check valves keep the two pressures permanently separate
exp: The double hanger yoke allows transfilling, gas flowing from a higher- to a lower-pressure cylinder. On a two-cylinder system, the gauge location means individual cylinder pressures can't be differentiated. Open both and you lose track of your true reserve.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 7, 9 (PDF p. 4, 5)

q: A person with 1,000 ohms of resistance contacts a 120 V source. Standing in a saline puddle cuts resistance to 500 ohms. What happens to the current?
c: It doubles, from 120 mA to 240 mA
It halves, from 120 mA to 60 mA
It stays at 120 mA
It rises from 12 mA to 24 mA
exp: I = E / R. 120 / 1,000 = 0.12 A (120 mA); 120 / 500 = 0.24 A (240 mA). Halving resistance doubles current, which is why spilled fluids make the OR electrically hazardous.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 26, 30 (PDF p. 13, 15)

q: After a circuit is rebuilt, the reservoir bag sits between the patient and the expiratory valve. Which rule does this break, and what is the consequence?
c: The absorber must be on the bag side; compound A results
The APL must not sit between the patient and inspiratory valve; hypoxemia results
The bag must not sit between the patient and either valve; rebreathing results
The fresh gas inlet must not sit between the patient and expiratory valve; barotrauma results
exp: Three arrangements must be avoided to prevent rebreathing, including the reservoir bag between the patient and the inspiratory or expiratory valve. A bag in that position becomes a reservoir of exhaled gas.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 20 (PDF p. 10)

q: A fluid warmer plugged into the anesthesia machine's convenience outlet trips its circuit breaker. What is the likely effect?
c: The O2 fail-safe valve closes
The whole machine shuts down immediately
The machine switches to battery for the rest of the case
The outlet circuit loses power, while the machine's own supply is protected
exp: The machine has several circuit breakers, generally protecting separate circuits for the AC supply, the battery, and the convenience receptacles. A tripped outlet breaker cuts that circuit without taking down the workstation.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 25 (PDF p. 13)

q: A closed claim involves a patient harmed by a gas delivery problem. Based on the lecture, which contributing cause is most likely?
c: Hospital pipeline failure alone
Spontaneous failure of a well-maintained machine
Human error, often combined with other factors
Manufacturer design defect
exp: Most adverse events are multifactorial, and human error is responsible for the majority, often through failure to check equipment, unfamiliarity, haste, inattention, distraction, or fatigue.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 17, 18 (PDF p. 9)

q: If a certain AC current is enough to cause ventricular fibrillation, about how much DC would be needed to do the same?
c: About one-third as much
About the same amount
About three times as much
About ten times as much
exp: It takes approximately three times as much DC as AC to cause ventricular fibrillation. That still doesn't make DC harmless.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 27 (PDF p. 14)

q: An intubated, paralyzed patient needs transport. Why is a Mapleson B or C with controlled ventilation acceptable here when it would be poor for a spontaneously breathing patient?
c: Mapleson A can't be used with an ETT
With controlled ventilation, the patient doesn't do the extra work of breathing
B and C don't allow rebreathing during controlled ventilation
B and C need less fresh gas than a Mapleson A
exp: B and C always permit rebreathing, so hyperventilation with FGF of 1.5-2.5 x MV is needed. In a spontaneously breathing patient, that raises metabolic work; controlled ventilation doesn't create that problem because the patient isn't doing the work. Mapleson A is for spontaneous breathing.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 21 (PDF p. 11)

q: Which items does the lecture identify as FUEL in the OR? Select 3.
c: Room air
Tracheal tubes
Fiberoptic light cords
Nitrous oxide
Gel mattress pads
Facial or body hair
exp: Fuel includes paper drapes, gauze dressings, tracheal tubes, gel mattress pads, and facial or body hair. N2O and air are oxidizers, and fiberoptic light cord ends are ignition sources.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 33 (PDF p. 17)

q: A spontaneously breathing patient with a minute ventilation of 8 L/min is transported on circuit 3 at 8 L/min fresh gas flow. Is that adequate?
c: No; circuit 3 needs about 12-20 L/min
Yes; it exceeds 0.7 x MV (5.6 L/min)
Yes; any FGF equal to MV prevents rebreathing
No; circuit 3 needs about 16-24 L/min
exp: Circuit 3 is the Mapleson C (fresh gas near the patient, no corrugated tubing), which always permits rebreathing and needs 1.5-2.5 x MV: 1.5 x 8 = 12 and 2.5 x 8 = 20 L/min. 0.7 x MV applies only to Mapleson A (circuit 1).
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 21 (PDF p. 11)

q: For an AC circuit, why can current be lower than E / R predicts?
c: Impedance adds capacitance and inductance, so Z exceeds R
Resistance itself falls whenever current alternates
AC voltage is always lower than DC voltage
Current in AC circuits can't be calculated
exp: For AC, Ohm's law is E = I x Z, where impedance is the sum of forces opposing electron movement: resistance plus capacitance and inductance. Using R alone overestimates current when those other components are significant.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 27 (PDF p. 14)

q: The pipeline fails, and the machine's O2 cylinder turns out to be empty. Which highlighted hypoxemia hazard is this?
c: Crossed hospital pipelines
Closed pipeline valves
Failure of the backup O2 reserve within the machine
Liquid O2 reservoir filled with nitrogen
exp: The cylinder is the machine's backup reserve; an empty or closed cylinder is a highlighted hazard usually caught on the machine check. The other options are upstream problems not highlighted as check items.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 4, 19 (PDF p. 2, 10)

q: An alcohol prep is still wet at the neck, O2 is flowing by nasal cannula under the drapes, and the surgeon picks up the cautery. Which single action removes an element of the fire triangle fastest?
c: Stop cautery until the prep dries and the O2 is reduced
Increase O2 flow to dilute the alcohol vapor
Switch the cannula to N2O
Cover the wet prep with a dry towel and proceed
exp: Wet flammable prep is fuel, pooled O2 is the oxidizer, and cautery is the ignition source. Holding the ignition source while the prep dries (lecture: let flammable prep dry before draping) and reducing O2 breaks the triangle. N2O is also an oxidizer, and a towel adds fuel.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 31, 33, 35 (PDF p. 16, 17, 18)

q: At 0400 on call, a provider rushes to finish before shift change and extubates before the patient is adequately awake. Which aggravating factors are at work? Select 2.
c: Fatigue
Lack of familiarity with equipment
Haste
Failure to check equipment
Standardized connectors
Redundant alarms
exp: Night call brings fatigue, and rushing to finish is haste; the lecture's haste example is extubating too early. Unfamiliarity and skipped checks aren't described here, and connectors and alarms are protective.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 18 (PDF p. 9)

q: After a power failure, you switch to a Mapleson C with a spontaneously breathing patient (MV 6 L/min) running off an O2 E-cylinder that reads 1500 psig (about 520 L). About how long will the O2 last?
c: About 35-58 minutes
About 87 minutes
About 124 minutes
About 3 hours
exp: Mapleson C needs 1.5-2.5 x MV = 9-15 L/min. 520 L / 15 = about 35 min; 520 / 9 = about 58 min. That window is similar to the battery's roughly 40 minutes, which is why the lecture says to have the patient safely covered within about an hour.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 25, 32 (PDF p. 13, 16)
concept: Backup O2 duration on a Mapleson

q: Pressure climbs with each manual breath, the bag is hard to squeeze, and no gas reaches the patient. How does this differ from a disconnection?
c: Both cause high pressure, but occlusion is slower
They can't be told apart at the bag
Occlusion causes high pressure with no flow; disconnection causes low pressure
Occlusion causes low pressure; disconnection causes high pressure
exp: An occlusion (plastic wrap, a misconnected humidifier, a misplaced PEEP valve) blocks gas, so pressure rises without flow. A disconnection or leak lets gas escape, so pressures fall and the bag goes soft.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 22, 23 (PDF p. 11, 12)

q: Two of these unlabeled cylinder valves share pin-index position 1. Which ones? Select 2.
c: Valve 1
Valve 2
Valve 3
Valve 4
Valve 5
None of these valves share a position
exp: Air is 1,5 and carbon dioxide is 1,6, so both use position 1. On the chart they're valves 3 and 4, whose left holes sit at the same spot. Valve 1 is O2 (2,5), valve 2 is N2O (3,5), and valve 5 is Entonox (7).
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 7 (PDF p. 4)

q: On a machine with an outlet check valve, a positive-pressure test at the common gas outlet passes, yet a vaporizer leak is later found. Why did the test miss it?
c: Vaporizer leaks only occur during ventilation
The test was performed with the vaporizer turned on
Positive pressure seals vaporizer leaks temporarily
The check valve kept test pressure from reaching the vaporizer
exp: With an outlet check valve, pressure applied at the CGO closes the valve and never reaches the low-pressure components upstream, so a positive-pressure test can pass despite a leak. Those machines need a negative-pressure test.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 15 (PDF p. 8)

q: After an OR fire is out and the patient is stabilized, which risk management steps does the lecture list? Select 3.
c: Treat it as an adverse event and follow reporting requirements
Discard burned materials to prevent reignition
Preserve the scene
Wait until the next day to report
Resume the next case in the same room right away
Notify the hospital risk manager
exp: After a fire: preserve the scene, notify the risk manager, follow institutional reporting requirements, treat it as an adverse event, and conduct regular fire drills. Discarding materials destroys evidence, and delaying reporting skips the process.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 39 (PDF p. 20)

q: During the machine check, a cylinder regulator's outlet gauge reads 180 psi instead of about 45. What does this mean?
c: The cylinder is overfilled and the reading is expected
The regulator has failed, sending near-cylinder pressure downstream
The inlet and outlet gauges are simply reversed
The pipeline is feeding back through the regulator
exp: The regulator's job is to turn variable high inlet pressure (up to about 2200 psi) into a constant low outlet (about 45 psi). The inlet gauge varies with cylinder contents; the outlet shouldn't. A high outlet reading means the regulator isn't regulating, which Dr. Elmore's lecture notes risks machine damage and barotrauma.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 10, 24 (PDF p. 5, 12)

q: A defibrillator delivers 360 joules over 0.01 seconds. What is the average power of the discharge?
c: 3.6 watts
360 watts
3,600 watts
36,000 watts
exp: Energy (joules) = power (watts) x time (seconds), so power = 360 J / 0.01 s = 36,000 W. 3.6 comes from multiplying by the time instead of dividing.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 26 (PDF p. 13)

q: To reduce airway fire risk, a resident suggests switching from 100% O2 to 50% O2 / 50% N2O. What is the problem?
c: The mixture is hypoxic
N2O is an equally good oxidizer, so risk is essentially unchanged
N2O is flammable fuel, so risk doubles
N2O raises the ignition temperature, lowering risk
exp: O2 and N2O function equally well as oxidizers; a 50/50 mixture supports combustion about as avidly as 100% O2. The lecture's prevention list says to keep O2 as low as possible and avoid N2O; lowering the oxidizer means using air.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 33, 35 (PDF p. 17, 18)

q: During spontaneous ventilation with a closed scavenging interface, hospital vacuum fails and the interface's positive-pressure relief valve is also stuck. What happens in the breathing circuit?
c: Negative pressure pulls the reservoir bag flat
Nothing, because the APL vents directly to the room
Fresh gas flow stops automatically
Pressure builds, because waste gas can't leave through the APL
exp: Slide 23 lists malfunction of the interface positive-pressure relief valve among causes of high breathing-system pressure during spontaneous ventilation. With vacuum failed and that valve stuck, gas leaving the APL backs up into the circuit. Negative pressure is the excessive-suction problem.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 20, 23 (PDF p. 10, 12)

q: Leadership debates buying a spare electronic vaporizer for every OR versus relying on TIVA during outages. Which risk management step is this?
c: Monitoring outcomes after changes are made
Defining the potential problems at hand
Weighing the benefits of expending available resources
Applying solutions to the identified problem
exp: Deciding whether a costly measure is worth it, given how likely and harmful the problem is, is weighing the benefits of expending resources. It comes after defining the problem and estimating likelihood, and before applying a solution.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 16 (PDF p. 8)

q: On battery power during an outage, the machine displays battery voltage falling through 11 V. What is the significance?
c: The battery has recharged and is stable
Total shutdown is close, since power cuts off below about 10 V
Only the convenience outlets will lose power
The ventilator will switch to a reserve battery
exp: When battery voltage drops below about 10 V, all power to the machine ceases to prevent deep discharge, taking the monitors, alarms, and ventilator with it. At 11 V, your Mapleson and TIVA alternatives should already be running.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 25 (PDF p. 13)

q: A classmate says, '0.23-0.4% of ASA closed claims involved gas delivery equipment: 115 of 6,000.' What is wrong with that statement?
c: 115/6,000 is about 1.9%; 0.23-0.4% is event incidence
115/6,000 is about 0.02%, far lower than stated
Nothing; the two figures agree exactly as stated
The database held 60,000 claims, not 6,000
exp: 115 / 6,000 is about 1.9% of claims. The slide notes present the 0.23-0.4% separately as the estimated incidence of equipment-related events. The audio summary links the two numbers, which don't match arithmetically.
disc: The lecture audio says 115 of about 6,000 claims is 'about 0.23-0.4%.' The arithmetic gives about 1.9%; the written notes list 0.23-0.4% as the estimated event incidence.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 17 (PDF p. 9)

q: Which scheduled case should be identified as the highest fire risk during preparation?
c: Cataract surgery with topical anesthesia and no cautery
Laparoscopic cholecystectomy under GA with a cuffed ETT
Knee arthroscopy under spinal with room air
Facial procedure under MAC with nasal cannula O2 and cautery
exp: High risk means the ignition source is near an open oxidizer: cautery around the face with O2 flowing by cannula under drapes. The lecture singles out open O2 delivery near the airway for extra caution.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 34, 35 (PDF p. 17, 18)

q: Given how rarely OR fires occur, which preparation measure most directly addresses the lecture's concern that providers lack experience responding?
c: Adding more fire extinguishers to each OR
Regular fire drills with assigned roles
Reporting fires to the risk manager
Using only laser-resistant ETTs
exp: Rarity is itself a hazard: providers aren't experienced or trained to respond. The lecture's preparation list answers that with training, fire drills, and assigning each person a task, so the response is practiced before it's needed.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 16, 34 (PDF p. 8, 17)

q: Slide 19 lists 'incorrect cylinder on oxygen yoke' as a hypoxemia hazard. For it to happen, what else has usually gone wrong?
c: The fail-safe valve was disconnected
The pin-index system was bypassed or damaged
The flowmeter sequence was reversed
The DISS pipeline fitting failed
exp: PISS pins on the yoke only accept cylinders with matching holes, so a wrong cylinder on the O2 yoke usually means the pins were removed, broken, or bypassed. The lecture warns this could result in hypoxic gas mixtures.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 7, 19 (PDF p. 4, 10)

q: A spontaneously breathing patient is on a Mapleson A at 1 x minute ventilation, but the tubing between the patient and bag is very short. What problem remains?
c: Exhaled CO2 can reach the bag and be rebreathed
FGF is too high and causes barotrauma
The circuit becomes a Mapleson C
No problem, since FGF exceeds 0.7 x MV
exp: Mapleson A needs two things: FGF of at least 0.7 x MV AND tubing long enough that exhaled CO2 doesn't reach the reservoir bag. Adequate flow alone doesn't fix tubing that's too short.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 21 (PDF p. 11)

q: Which connections fit the standard common gas outlet? Select 2.
c: A 22 mm male connector inserted inside the outlet
A 19 mm conical scavenging fitting
A 15 mm male connector inserted inside the outlet
A 15 mm female connector fitted over the outside
A 30 mm conical scavenging hose
A 22 mm female connector fitted over the outside
exp: The CGO has a 15 mm internal (female) diameter and 22 mm external (male) diameter, so a 15 mm male fitting goes inside and a 22 mm female fitting goes over the outside. 19 and 30 mm conical fittings are reserved for scavenging.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 15 (PDF p. 8)

q: Per the lecture notes, who usually identifies the fire extinguisher location during time-out and can activate the fire alarm?
c: The surgeon
The scrub tech
The circulating nurse
The anesthesia provider
exp: Slide 38 notes: during time-out, the circulating nurse is usually the one who identifies the fire extinguisher location and can activate the fire alarm. Everyone has an assigned task: anesthesia controls gases and the airway, and the surgeon stops the ignition source.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 34, 38 (PDF p. 17, 19)

q: Using the lecture's Ohm's-law model of gas flow, what happens at a fixed knob position if the pressure at the flow control valve inlet doubles from 16 psi?
c: Flow stops, since the fail-safe closes
Flow is unchanged, since the orifice is fixed
Flow roughly doubles
Flow halves, since resistance doubles
exp: Flow = pressure / resistance. With the orifice (resistance) unchanged, doubling the driving pressure roughly doubles flow. That's why stable regulated pressure at the flow control valves matters for flowmeter accuracy.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 5, 13 (PDF p. 3, 7)

q: Why is the ESU return electrode made large while the active pencil tip is small?
c: The large pad supplies more current back to the tip
A large pad lowers the frequency of the ESU current
The pad's size prevents ESU interference with monitors
Tip concentrates current to cut; the large pad disperses it to avoid burns
exp: Current is concentrated at the small active tip to cut or coagulate, then exits through the large dispersive pad, which spreads it over a big area of skin. That's why poor pad contact, which shrinks the contact area, causes burns.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 31 (PDF p. 16)

q: A spontaneously breathing patient (MV 6 L/min) is moved from circuit 2 to circuit 1. How does the minimum fresh gas flow change?
c: From about 9 L/min to about 4.2 L/min
From about 4.2 L/min to about 9 L/min
From about 15 L/min to about 6 L/min
It doesn't change; both need 1.5 x MV
exp: Circuit 2 is the Mapleson B: at least 1.5 x MV = 9 L/min (up to 15). Circuit 1 is the Mapleson A (fresh gas at the bag end), the spontaneous-breathing circuit: at least 0.7 x MV = 4.2 L/min.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 21 (PDF p. 11)
concept: Mapleson B to A flow change

q: Which statements correctly compare an airway fire with a fire on the patient? Select 2.
c: Airway fire: extinguish with a CO2 extinguisher into the airway first
Airway fire: remove the tube and stop gases simultaneously
Fire on the patient: leave the drapes in place to smother the fire
Airway fire: keep ventilating with 100% O2 while removing the tube
Fire on the patient: assess the patient before stopping gases
Fire on the patient: turn off gases, then remove drapes and burning materials
exp: Airway fire: simultaneously remove the tube and stop gases, then saline and remove burning material. Fire on the patient: turn off gases, remove drapes and burning materials, extinguish with water, saline, or an extinguisher, then assess. Continuing O2 feeds the fire.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 36, 37 (PDF p. 18, 19)

q: A machine delivers sevoflurane only through a GE Aladin cassette. After the battery is exhausted in a prolonged outage, how can anesthesia be maintained?
c: Use the O2 flush to push agent through the cassette
IV anesthesia (TIVA), since the Aladin can't deliver agent without power
Continue the Aladin at its last setting, since it's mechanical
Turn the Aladin cassette upside down to release agent
exp: Electronic vaporizers such as the GE Aladin can't deliver agent without electrical power. Once the battery is gone, only emergency O2 and conventional mechanical vaporizers remain; on an Aladin machine that means switching to TIVA, with ventilation by Mapleson.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 32 (PDF p. 16)

q: Which pairings of hazard to lecture list are correct? Select 2.
c: Apnea (failure to start ventilation): hypercarbia list
Exhausted absorbent: hypoxemia list
Closed O2 cylinder valve: hypercarbia list
Increased apparatus dead space: hypoxemia list
Crossed hospital pipelines: hypercarbia list
Inadequate ventilation: hypoxemia list
exp: Inadequate ventilation appears on the hypoxemia list (highlighted), and apnea from failure to initiate or continue controlled ventilation heads the hypercarbia list. Crossed pipelines and a closed cylinder are hypoxemia hazards; absorbent and dead space are hypercarbia hazards.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 19, 20 (PDF p. 10)

q: A fire can't be extinguished and the team evacuates the OR. What does the lecture say about the room door?
c: Prop it open for firefighters
Open and close it to vent smoke
Close it and don't reopen it
Leave it ajar to monitor the fire
exp: Failure to extinguish: use a CO2 extinguisher, activate the fire alarm, consider evacuation (close the door and don't reopen it), and turn off the medical gas supply to the room.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slide 38 (PDF p. 19)

q: Pipeline and cylinder pressures are normal, yet inspired O2 is falling. Which hazard would a supply-pressure alarm NOT detect?
c: Closed pipeline valve
O2 flowmeter turned off
Disconnected O2 hose
Empty O2 cylinder with a failed pipeline
exp: Supply-pressure alarms respond to O2 pressure. A flowmeter turned off leaves supply pressure normal while O2 delivery stops. A disconnected hose, a closed pipeline valve, or an empty backup with a failed pipeline all drop supply pressure.
ref: Anesthesia Workstation Hazards & Safety (McPherson): slides 4, 19 (PDF p. 2, 10)

Individuals, not systems, cause adverse events
exp: The slide shows factors combining through the system and the individual into an event, 'part of the chain of events.' It matches the incidence slide: most adverse events are multifactorial.
